01_giris: For the last hundred years, it was banned.
It was forbidden in schools, its books were confiscated, and even its name was not to be spoken.
But that language did not fall silent.
It lived on in mothers' lullabies, in the songs of the dengbêj, and in the dim rooms of the madrasas.
Despite oppression, bans and assimilation, it did not disappear.
This language is, without doubt, the ancient language of Mesopotamia: Kurdish.
Spoken today by more than forty million people, let us explore its origins, its relatives, its unique grammar, and the scholars who kept it alive for centuries.
02_dil_ailesi: Kurdish belongs to the Indo-European family, the largest language family in the world.
Within the Indo-Iranian branch of this family, it is part of the Iranian languages.
More precisely, it belongs to the Northwestern Iranian group.
Its closest relatives are Balochi and Talysh.
Persian comes from the same family but sits on a different branch: the Southwestern Iranian group.
So Kurdish and Persian are not siblings, but cousins.
Pashto and Ossetian are more distant members of this large family.
One of the most famous historical branches of this family is the Scythians.
Although some historians in Turkey, with a forced claim, present the Scythians as Turks, this view is not supported by linguistic evidence.
The personal names, place names and words left by the Scythians show that their language belonged to the Eastern Iranian group.
Today's Ossetian is considered the living descendant of the Scythian language.
Traces of this family bond can be seen even in European languages.
The Kurdish word "stêr", meaning star, is related to English "star" and Latin "stella".
The Kurdish word "nû", meaning new, shares its root with English "new"; and "nav", meaning name, with "name".
03_arkaik: Kurdish has carried many features of the ancient Iranian languages into the present day.
Some linguists argue that, in terms of its archaic vocabulary, Kurdish may be older than Persian.
04_eril_disil: One of the most striking features of Kurdish is grammatical gender.
In Kurmanji in particular, nouns are divided into masculine and feminine, and this distinction is reflected in the endings words take.
"Ez mêrî dibînim": I see the man.
"Ez jinê dibînim": I see the woman.
So, does this feature exist in other Iranian languages?
Persian lost grammatical gender centuries ago.
Yet Old Persian and Avestan did have this distinction.
Today, the languages that preserve gender include the Kurmanji, Zazaki and Gorani dialects of Kurdish, as well as Pashto and some Central Iranian dialects.
Kurdish still keeps alive this ancient heritage that Persian lost.
Another interesting aspect of Kurdish grammar is its ergative structure.
In the past tense, with transitive verbs, the structure of the sentence changes completely.
This is a feature found in relatively few languages in the world.
05_seslenme: In Kurdish, when you call out to someone, a suffix is added to the end of the noun.
In linguistics, this is called the vocative case.
Masculine nouns take "o", feminine nouns take "ê", and the plural takes "no".
This small suffix actually reveals something big.
The vocative case is a very old grammatical feature inherited from Proto-Indo-European.
Many languages, like Persian, have lost these endings and replaced them with a separate word such as "ey".
Kurdish, however, has preserved this ending for thousands of years.
It is one of the most vivid proofs of the archaic character of Kurdish.
06_lehceler: Kurds live in Bakur in the north, Başûr in the south, Rojava in the west and Rojhelat in the east.
There is no official census of the Kurdish population.
According to estimates, 23 to 35 million Kurds live in Bakur, 8 to 10 million in Rojhelat, 6 to 8 million in Başûr, and 2 to 3 million in Rojava.
Together with the Caucasus, Central Asia and the diaspora, the total population is estimated at between forty and sixty million.
The main dialects of Kurdish are: Kurmanji, or Northern Kurdish.
It is the most widely spoken dialect.
It is spoken in Bakur and Rojava, in the north of Başûr, in parts of Rojhelat and in the Caucasus.
Sorani, or Central Kurdish.
It is widespread in Başûr and Rojhelat.
Southern Kurdish.
Kalhuri, Feyli and Laki belong to this group.
Zazaki, also called Kirmancki and Dimili.
It is spoken across a wide area, above all in Dersim, Çewlîg, Xarpêt, Amed and Sêwreg.
And Gorani, also called Hawrami.
It is one of the oldest written languages of classical Kurdish literature.
It was used as a literary language at the courts of Ardalan and Baban.
This diversity of dialects has given Kurdish a great richness of vocabulary.
Different words are used for the same concept in different regions.
Creating new words with prefixes and suffixes is also remarkably easy.
Its vocabulary for nature, herding, mountains and farming reflects a way of life thousands of years old.
07_petersburg: In the years to come, Kurdish would face bans, denial and oppression in its own lands.
Yet far away, Russian linguists were already showing great interest in this language in the nineteenth century.
Saint Petersburg had become a true center of Kurdology.
The Russian academic Pyotr Lerch published extensive studies on Kurdish in the 1850s.
Aleksandr Jaba, the Russian consul in Erzurum, worked with Kurdish scholars and collected a large number of Kurdish manuscripts.
His Kurdish-French dictionary was published in 1879 by the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Petersburg.
One of the most valuable works in these Petersburg collections belongs to the great Kurdish poet and thinker Ehmedê Xanî.
In 1683, Xanî wrote a rhymed Kurdish-Arabic dictionary to help children learn the language: "Nûbihara Biçûkan", meaning The Children's Spring.
Manuscripts of this work are preserved today in the Petersburg collections.
This tradition continued in the Soviet era.
Kurdologists such as Margarita Rudenko studied Xanî's immortal work "Mem û Zîn", translated it into Russian, and catalogued Kurdish manuscripts for future generations.
08_medreseler: For centuries, the madrasas of the Kurdish lands were not merely institutions of religious education.
They were also schools of language, literature, logic and astronomy.
Although most textbooks were in Arabic, the language of teaching, explanation and commentary was Kurdish.
Students began with Ehmedê Xanî's work Nûbihar, and read Melayê Cizîrî's Dîwan and Melayê Bateyî's Mewlûd.
Kurdish became the carrier of learning.
These madrasas gave great scholars to the Islamic world.
Poets and thinkers such as Melayê Cizîrî, Feqiyê Teyran and Ehmedê Xanî emerged from this tradition.
Molla Gürani, teacher of Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, and in more recent times Mela Xelîlê Sêrtî, were also nourished by these roots.
The Kurdish madrasas became one of the most important strongholds keeping the written tradition of the language alive.
09_bediuzzaman: One of the best-known figures raised by this madrasa tradition is Bediüzzaman Said Nursi.
Born in the village of Nurs in Bedlîs, Said Nursi was educated in madrasas that taught in Kurdish.
For the university he dreamed of founding in the East, Medresetü'z-Zehra, he set out his language formula: "Arabî vâcib, Kürdî câiz, Türkî lâzım."
That is: Arabic obligatory, Kurdish permitted, Turkish necessary.
Said Nursi also wrote in Kurdish.
In 1908, an article of his in Kurdish appeared in the Kürd Teâvün ve Terakkî newspaper published in Istanbul.
The place of Kurdish in his scholarly life is seen most strikingly in his commentary İşaratü'l-İ'caz.
This work was written at the front during the First World War.
According to his students, the Master first explained the verses in Kurdish to those around him, and his student Molla Habib quickly wrote these explanations down in Arabic.
It is said that Arabic was chosen because philosophical currents denying the existence of God were gaining ground at the time.
The Master wanted to reach many more people across the Islamic world quickly, without the need for translation.
In later years, Said Nursi wrote most of his works in Ottoman Turkish to reach a wider audience.
But the depth of his collected works came from the depth of his intellectual world.
And the source that nourished that world was the language he had read, thought and taught in for years: Kurdish.
10_kapanis: With its words surviving from antiquity, its masculine and feminine distinction, its vocative endings, its rich dialects and its deep-rooted written tradition, Kurdish is not merely a means of communication.
It is a memory thousands of years old.
And this memory lives on in every mouth that speaks it.
